topic.title: Osmosis, plasmolysis and turgidity
topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: Osmosis is asked every year, in two places. On the B2 paper it is a whole question of about 6 to 8 marks: Summer 2024 Higher Q3 gave [2] for choosing the right description and explanation from two lists, [2] for describing and explaining a change in liquid level, [2] for the vacuole and the cytoplasm and [1] for the cell membrane. In Unit 7 it is Prescribed Practical B5 itself — Summer 2025's Booklet A task was potato and parsnip cylinders in sucrose, with percentage changes in mass to one decimal place, the variables table and turgid or plasmolysed cells.
mustMemorise: Osmosis: water molecules diffuse across a selectively permeable membrane, out of the dilute solution and into the one that is more concentrated
Turgid: the vacuole is full and pushes the membrane against the cell wall
Flaccid: the vacuole has shrunk and no longer pushes on the wall
Plasmolysed: the cell membrane has pulled away from the cell wall
The cell wall limits the entry of water, so plant cells do not burst
Percentage change in mass = change in mass ÷ mass at the start × 100
notOnThisSpec: Water potential, solute potential and pressure potential
The words hypotonic, hypertonic and isotonic
Active transport of water (water never moves by active transport)
Transpiration and the potometer, which are the next topic

Describe what happens to the vacuole, the cytoplasm and the cell membrane as a cell loses water
Explain that the cell wall limits the entry of water, so a plant cell does not burst
Say what happens to an animal cell in pure water and in a concentrated solution, and why it differs from a plant cell
Calculate a percentage change in mass to one decimal place, with its + or − sign
Read the concentration of no change from a graph of percentage change against concentration
Explain a result from Prescribed Practical B5 in terms of the concentrations on either side of the membrane
Say what happens with equal concentrations inside and outside (no net movement), and read it as the zero of the graph
Explain the results of weighed Visking bags in a range of outside concentrations
sheet.howExamined: B2, 1 hour 15 minutes: 70 marks at Foundation, 80 at Higher, calculator allowed. Osmosis usually opens a question with a diagram of an apparatus or a set of cells, then asks for a calculation and an explanation. Marks are single [1] lines with tight accept lists — 'plasmolysed' not 'shrunk', 'pulled away from the cell wall' not 'the wall moved'. The same content is Prescribed Practical B5, so it also appears in Unit 7 Booklet A as a task and in Booklet B as a written question about technique, variables and percentage change. Summer 2026 Higher Booklet B Q4 weighed four Visking bags of one solution in four outside concentrations and asked why a percentage, why one bag lost mass and what the inside concentration could be.
traps: Giving the general definition of osmosis when the question asks about this apparatus (Summer 2024 B2 Higher Q3)
Describing the concentration when the question asks about the level (Summer 2024 B2 Higher Q3)
Avoiding the word 'smaller' twice, for the vacuole and then the cytoplasm, and losing the second mark (Summer 2024 B2 Higher Q3)
Saying the cell wall moved away from the membrane, rather than the membrane away from the wall
Leaving the + or − off a change in mass (Summer 2025 Unit 7 Biology Booklet A)
Writing a percentage change as a whole number when one decimal place was asked for (Summer 2025 Unit 7 Biology Booklet A Higher)
Dividing the change in mass by the final mass instead of the starting mass
Saying sucrose passed through the membrane (Summer 2025 Unit 7 Biology Booklet A Foundation)
Confusing turgor with plasmolysis (Summer 2025 Unit 7 Biology Booklet A Higher)
Leaving the cell wall out of the answer to why a plant cell does not burst (Summer 2023 Unit 7 Biology Booklet B Higher Q4)
Writing a whole-number percentage change as 13 when the column asks for one decimal place: 13.0 is the answer, and the zero carries the mark (Summer 2025 Unit 7 Biology Booklet A Higher Q1)

Explaining a shrunken cell by saying the sucrose solution passed through the membrane: the membrane is selectively permeable, and what moves is water, out of the cell and into the stronger solution (Summer 2025 Unit 7 Biology Booklet A Foundation Q1)

noteBlocks.md: **Osmosis** is the diffusion of **water** molecules out of a **dilute** solution and into a **more concentrated** one, through a **selectively permeable membrane**. The membrane lets small molecules such as water through and holds large ones, such as sugar, back.

noteBlocks.title: Why water goes that way
noteBlocks.md: A dilute solution holds **more water** in each cubic centimetre, so more water molecules strike the membrane from that side each second. More cross one way than the other: the **net** movement is into the concentrated solution.

noteBlocks.stem: A selectively permeable membrane separates 5 per cent sugar solution from 20 per cent sugar solution. Say which way water moves, and whether the sugar moves. [2]

steps.working: Water moves from the 5 per cent side into the 20 per cent side.
steps.decision: The 5 per cent solution is the dilute one: more water per cubic centimetre, so more water crosses from it.

steps.working: The sugar does not cross.
steps.decision: Its molecules are too large for the membrane. Sugar spreading out would be diffusion, but it would not be osmosis, which is water only.

noteBlocks.task: Put a different number of particles on each side of the membrane and watch which way the net movement goes. Then say in one sentence why a carrot cylinder in pure water gains mass, using the words dilute, concentrated and selectively permeable.

noteBlocks.prompt: A selectively permeable membrane separates pure water from a 10 per cent salt solution. Which way does water move overall?
options: from the pure water into the salt solution
from the salt solution into the pure water
there is no overall movement
noteBlocks.answer: from the pure water into the salt solution
noteBlocks.explain: Pure water is the most dilute solution there is, so water moves from it into the salt solution, the more concentrated one. The See it moved water from 5 per cent into 20 per cent the same way.

optionNotes.option: from the salt solution into the pure water
optionNotes.why: It tempts because salt is the thing that seems to spread, but osmosis is water moving into the more concentrated solution.

optionNotes.option: there is no overall movement
optionNotes.why: No overall movement needs the two sides at the same concentration; pure water and salt solution are not.

twin.prompt: A selectively permeable membrane separates 2 per cent sucrose solution from 8 per cent sucrose solution. Which way does water move overall?
options: from the 2 per cent into the 8 per cent solution
from the 8 per cent into the 2 per cent solution
there is no overall movement
twin.answer: from the 2 per cent into the 8 per cent solution
twin.explain: The 2 per cent solution is the more dilute, so water moves out of it and into the 8 per cent solution.

optionNotes.option: from the 8 per cent into the 2 per cent solution
optionNotes.why: That is the reverse: water moves into the stronger solution, not out of it.

optionNotes.option: there is no overall movement
optionNotes.why: The two concentrations differ, so there is a net movement of water.

noteBlocks.md: A plant cell's sap is itself a solution. So always name **both** liquids, the cell sap and the solution outside, and decide which is the more concentrated.

Outside **weaker**: water moves in and the tissue gains mass. Outside **stronger**: water moves out and it loses mass. Outside **equal**: water still crosses both ways, but there is **no net movement**, so the mass does not change.

noteBlocks.stem: Three carrot cylinders are left in pure water, in a solution as concentrated as their cell sap, and in a stronger solution. Describe what happens to each, and why. [3]

steps.working: Pure water: water moves in and the cylinder gains mass.
steps.decision: The cell sap is the more concentrated of the two liquids.

steps.working: Equal solution: no net movement, so no change in mass.
steps.decision: Water crosses both ways at the same rate, so nothing changes overall.

steps.working: Stronger solution: water moves out and the cylinder loses mass.
steps.decision: Now the outside is the more concentrated liquid.

noteBlocks.prompt: A potato cylinder neither gains nor loses mass in a 0.3 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution. What does that tell you?
options: its cell sap is about as concentrated as 0.3 mol dm⁻³ sucrose
osmosis has stopped completely in its cells
its membranes have stopped letting water through
noteBlocks.answer: its cell sap is about as concentrated as 0.3 mol dm⁻³ sucrose
noteBlocks.explain: No change in mass means no net movement of water, and that happens when the cell sap and the solution are equally concentrated. Water still crosses both ways, as in the equal case of the See it.

optionNotes.option: osmosis has stopped completely in its cells
optionNotes.why: Water still crosses the membrane both ways; it is only the net movement that is zero.

optionNotes.option: its membranes have stopped letting water through
optionNotes.why: The membranes still let water through; equal concentrations make the movement balance.

twin.prompt: A potato cylinder loses mass in a 0.5 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution. What does that tell you about its cell sap?
options: it is more dilute than 0.5 mol dm⁻³ sucrose
it is more concentrated than 0.5 mol dm⁻³ sucrose
it is as concentrated as 0.5 mol dm⁻³ sucrose
twin.answer: it is more dilute than 0.5 mol dm⁻³ sucrose
twin.explain: Water left the cells, so it moved towards the solution: the solution outside was the more concentrated, and the cell sap the more dilute.

optionNotes.option: it is more concentrated than 0.5 mol dm⁻³ sucrose
optionNotes.why: If the sap were the stronger, water would have moved in and the cylinder gained mass.

optionNotes.option: it is as concentrated as 0.5 mol dm⁻³ sucrose
optionNotes.why: Equal concentrations give no change in mass; this cylinder lost mass.

noteBlocks.md: A cell that takes in water is **turgid**: its vacuole is full and presses the cytoplasm and membrane against the cell wall. Many turgid cells pressing on their neighbours make a plant firm.

A cell that loses a lot of water is **plasmolysed**: the vacuole and cytoplasm get **smaller** and the **membrane pulls away from the cell wall**. The wall, rigid cellulose, does not move. In between, the cell is limp (flaccid), but CCEA's papers name only turgid and plasmolysed.

noteBlocks.prompt: The examiner shows you this and asks what has happened to the cell membrane. What is the one sentence that earns the mark — and why is 'the cell wall has pulled away' not it?

noteBlocks.stem: A drawing shows a cell from a celery stalk left in a strong salt solution. Give two features of the drawing that show it has lost water. [2]

steps.working: The cell membrane has pulled away from the cell wall.
steps.decision: Name the moving part first: the membrane, never the wall.

steps.working: The vacuole is small.
steps.decision: A second, separate feature earns the second mark; the cytoplasm being smaller would do as well.

noteBlocks.title: GCSE Biology Revision "Osmosis"
noteBlocks.why: A second look at cells gaining and losing water, beside the worked features.

noteBlocks.prompt: In the photograph of red onion cells in a strong solution, which structure has moved?
options: the cell membrane, pulling away from the wall
the cell wall, pulling away from the membrane
both, pulling away from each other
noteBlocks.answer: the cell membrane, pulling away from the wall
noteBlocks.explain: The walls keep their straight sides because rigid cellulose does not move; the shrinking contents pull the membrane inwards, away from the wall. The See it's first feature named the membrane in the same way.

optionNotes.option: the cell wall, pulling away from the membrane
optionNotes.why: The walls keep their shape in the photograph; it is the contents and their membrane that shrink.

optionNotes.option: both, pulling away from each other
optionNotes.why: Only the contents shrink; the rigid wall stays where it was.

twin.prompt: A plant cell has become plasmolysed. What has happened to the size of its vacuole?
options: it has become smaller
it has become larger
it has stayed the same
twin.explain: Water has left the vacuole by osmosis, so it has shrunk, and so has the cytoplasm.

optionNotes.option: it has become larger
optionNotes.why: A larger vacuole is what a turgid cell has; a plasmolysed cell has lost water.

optionNotes.option: it has stayed the same
optionNotes.why: The water that left came out of the vacuole and cytoplasm, so they shrink.

noteBlocks.md: A plasmolysed cell put into **pure water** recovers. Now the cell sap is the **more concentrated** liquid, so water moves **in**: the vacuole and cytoplasm swell, the membrane presses back against the wall, and the cell becomes **turgid**.
A full answer has three parts: water moves **in**, **across the selectively permeable membrane**, **from the dilute solution to the more concentrated** one.

noteBlocks.stem: Celery cells plasmolysed in strong salt solution are then put into pure water. Explain how osmosis changes the cells. [3]

steps.working: Water moves into the cells.
steps.decision: The pure water outside is the dilute liquid; the cell sap is the concentrated one.

steps.working: It crosses the selectively permeable cell membrane.
steps.decision: Naming the membrane's property is a mark of its own.

steps.working: It moves from the dilute water to the more concentrated sap, so the vacuole swells and the cells become turgid.
steps.decision: Direction, then result: the membrane returns to the wall.

noteBlocks.prompt: Plasmolysed onion cells are put into pure water for an hour. Which describes them afterwards?
options: turgid, with the membrane pressed against the wall
plasmolysed, with the membrane still away from the wall
burst, with the cell wall split open
noteBlocks.answer: turgid, with the membrane pressed against the wall
noteBlocks.explain: The cell sap is now more concentrated than the pure water, so water moves in, the vacuole swells and the membrane presses back on the wall: turgid. The celery cells in the See it recovered the same way.

optionNotes.option: plasmolysed, with the membrane still away from the wall
optionNotes.why: That ignores the new surroundings: in pure water the sap is the stronger liquid, so water comes back in.

optionNotes.option: burst, with the cell wall split open
optionNotes.why: The cell wall limits the entry of water, so a plant cell becomes turgid rather than bursting.

twin.prompt: Turgid potato cells are put into a strong sucrose solution for an hour. Which describes them afterwards?
options: plasmolysed, with the membrane pulled away from the wall
turgid, with the membrane pressed against the wall
burst, with the membrane split
twin.answer: plasmolysed, with the membrane pulled away from the wall
twin.explain: The sucrose solution is more concentrated than the sap, so water leaves, the contents shrink and the membrane pulls away from the wall.

optionNotes.option: turgid, with the membrane pressed against the wall
optionNotes.why: They stay turgid only in a weaker solution; this one is stronger, so water leaves.

optionNotes.option: burst, with the membrane split
optionNotes.why: Cells burst only when too much water enters; here water is leaving.

noteBlocks.text: 5. Why a plant cell does not burst

noteBlocks.md: In pure water, a plant cell takes in water until it is turgid. The **cell wall** will then stretch no further, so it **limits the entry of water** and the cell does not burst.
An animal cell, such as a red blood cell, has **no cell wall**. Water keeps entering until the membrane bursts. In a concentrated solution the same animal cell loses water and shrinks.

noteBlocks.stem: A spinach leaf cell and a red blood cell are each put into pure water. Describe and explain what happens to each. [4]

steps.working: Water moves into both cells by osmosis.
steps.decision: Pure water is more dilute than the contents of either cell.

steps.working: The red blood cell swells and bursts.
steps.decision: Nothing outside its membrane stops it stretching.

steps.working: The spinach cell becomes turgid but does not burst,
steps.decision: Name the result for the plant cell before the reason.

steps.working: because its cell wall limits the entry of water.
steps.decision: The wall is the one structure the red blood cell lacks.

noteBlocks.prompt: A turgid plant cell in pure water takes in no more water. Which statement explains why?
options: its cell wall will not stretch any further, so it limits the entry of water
its cell membrane has stopped letting water through
its vacuole has stopped osmosis
noteBlocks.answer: its cell wall will not stretch any further, so it limits the entry of water
noteBlocks.explain: The rigid wall pushes back once the cell is full, so no more water can enter and the cell cannot burst. In the See it the spinach cell stopped at turgid for that reason.

optionNotes.option: its cell membrane has stopped letting water through
optionNotes.why: The membrane still lets water through; it is the wall that stops the cell swelling further.

optionNotes.option: its vacuole has stopped osmosis
optionNotes.why: The vacuole is where the water goes; it does not control the membrane or the wall.

twin.prompt: A red blood cell is put into pure water and bursts. Which statement explains why?
options: it has no cell wall to limit the entry of water
sugar from the water enters and splits it
its vacuole fills and splits
twin.answer: it has no cell wall to limit the entry of water
twin.explain: Water keeps entering by osmosis, and with no wall to push back the membrane stretches until it bursts.

optionNotes.option: sugar from the water enters and splits it
optionNotes.why: Pure water has no sugar in it; it is water entering by osmosis that swells the cell.

optionNotes.option: its vacuole fills and splits
optionNotes.why: A red blood cell has no large vacuole; the whole cell swells until its membrane bursts.

noteBlocks.md: In Prescribed Practical B5 the cylinders rarely start at the same mass, so a raw change in grams cannot be compared fairly. A **percentage change** compares each change with its own starting mass.
**percentage change = change in mass ÷ mass at the start × 100**. Give the change its **+** or **−** sign, and round to one decimal place, keeping a trailing zero: 14.0, never 14.

noteBlocks.stem: A potato cylinder of 2.50 g weighs 2.85 g when it comes out of water the next day. Find the percentage change, correct to 1 decimal place. [2]

steps.working: Change in mass = 2.85 − 2.50 = +0.35 g
steps.decision: Final minus start, so the sign shows a gain.
Divide by the mass at the start; write the trailing zero for one decimal place.

noteBlocks.prompt: A 3.20 g potato cylinder weighs 2.88 g after a day in strong sugar solution. Give the percentage change, correct to 1 decimal place.
noteBlocks.explain: Change = 2.88 − 3.20 = −0.32 g, and −0.32 ÷ 3.20 × 100 = −10.0 per cent. The divisor is the starting mass, as in the See it, and the minus sign shows a loss.

Where the line crosses zero there is no change in mass, so the cell sap is **as concentrated as** that solution. That reading is how the practical finds the concentration of the cell sap.

noteBlocks.stem: Use the graph to find the concentration of sucrose solution with the same concentration as the potato's cell sap, and explain your answer. [2]

steps.working: The line crosses zero at 6 per cent.
steps.decision: Read along the zero line, then down to the concentration axis.

steps.working: No change in mass there, so no net movement of water: the sap is as concentrated as 6 per cent sucrose.
steps.decision: Zero change means equal concentrations, not that osmosis has stopped.

noteBlocks.prompt: On the graph of potato cylinders in sucrose solutions, what happens to a cylinder in 12 per cent sucrose?
options: it loses mass, and its cells become plasmolysed
it gains mass, and its cells become turgid
its mass does not change
noteBlocks.answer: it loses mass, and its cells become plasmolysed
noteBlocks.explain: At 12 per cent the line is below zero, so the cylinder loses mass: the solution is stronger than the sap, water leaves, and the cells plasmolyse. The See it found the sap matches 6 per cent; anything stronger draws water out.

optionNotes.option: it gains mass, and its cells become turgid
optionNotes.why: Gains are above the zero line; at 12 per cent the line is well below it.

optionNotes.option: its mass does not change
optionNotes.why: No change is only where the line crosses zero, at 6 per cent.

twin.prompt: On the same graph, what happens to a cylinder in 2 per cent sucrose?
options: it gains mass, and its cells become turgid
it loses mass, and its cells become plasmolysed
its mass does not change
twin.answer: it gains mass, and its cells become turgid
twin.explain: At 2 per cent the line is above zero: the solution is weaker than the sap, so water enters and the cells become turgid.

optionNotes.option: it loses mass, and its cells become plasmolysed
optionNotes.why: Losses are below the zero line; at 2 per cent the line is above it.

optionNotes.option: its mass does not change
optionNotes.why: No change is only at 6 per cent, where the line crosses zero.

noteBlocks.stem: Three bags stand in 5 per cent sucrose for 24 hours. Bag 1 (water inside) goes from 20.4 g to 18.8 g, bag 2 (5 per cent) stays at 20.9 g, bag 3 (20 per cent) goes from 21.6 g to 24.4 g. Explain the three results. [3]

steps.working: Bag 1: −1.6 g, −7.8 per cent. The outside is stronger, so water leaves the bag.
steps.decision: Water moves out through the tubing into the more concentrated solution.

steps.working: Bag 2: 0.0 g, 0.0 per cent. Inside and outside are equal, so there is no net movement.
steps.decision: Equal concentrations: the third case, as for the potato.

steps.working: Bag 3: +2.8 g, +13.0 per cent. The inside is stronger, so water enters.
steps.decision: The sucrose stays inside; only water crosses the tubing.

noteBlocks.prompt: Four Visking bags hold the same sucrose solution and stand in 0, 5, 10 and 15 per cent sucrose. Their percentage changes in mass are +31, +12, −6 and −15. What could the concentration inside the bags be?

between 0 and 5 per cent
between 10 and 15 per cent
noteBlocks.explain: The bags gain mass up to 5 per cent and lose it from 10 per cent, so the change crosses zero between them: the inside matches a concentration between 5 and 10 per cent. In the See it, the bag that matched its outside did not change.

optionNotes.why: Bags still gained mass at 5 per cent, so the inside was stronger than 5 per cent.

optionNotes.option: between 10 and 15 per cent
optionNotes.why: Bags already lost mass at 10 per cent, so the inside was weaker than 10 per cent.

twin.prompt: In the same set of four bags, why did the bag in 10 per cent sucrose lose mass?
options: water moved out of it into the more concentrated 10 per cent solution
sucrose moved out of it into the beaker
water moved into it from the 10 per cent solution
twin.answer: water moved out of it into the more concentrated 10 per cent solution
twin.explain: The 10 per cent outside was stronger than the inside, so water left the bag through the selectively permeable tubing.

optionNotes.option: sucrose moved out of it into the beaker
optionNotes.why: Sucrose molecules are too large to cross the tubing; only water moves.

optionNotes.option: water moved into it from the 10 per cent solution
optionNotes.why: Water moving in would make the bag gain mass; it lost mass.

steps.decision: The membrane has come away from the wall, which is what plasmolysed means.

steps.decision: Direction first, then the membrane named with its property.

options: Because the cell sap is now more concentrated than the pure water outside
Because sucrose leaves the cells into the water
Because the cell wall pumps water in
whyMenu.explain: In pure water the sap is the stronger solution, so water moves in by osmosis. Sucrose does not cross the membrane, and the wall does no pumping.

steps.decision: Dilute to concentrated earns the last mark; the result shows where it leads.

twin.stem: A cell like the one in the diagram is left in pure water for an hour. Which term describes it afterwards?

options.feedback: Water enters, the vacuole swells and the membrane presses back on the wall.
That was its state before; in pure water the sap is the stronger liquid, so water comes back in.
The cell wall limits the entry of water, so a plant cell does not burst.

items.stem: Before we start, three things from B1. Which structure controls what enters and leaves a cell?

options.feedback: The membrane. Everything in this topic happens across it.
The wall is outside the membrane and gives support. The membrane is the one that chooses what crosses.
The vacuole stores cell sap. Controlling entry and exit is the membrane's job.
The nucleus holds the chromosomes and controls the cell's activities, not what crosses its edge.

items.stem: Which structure does a plant cell have that an animal cell does not?

options.feedback: The cell wall — and it turns out to be the reason a plant cell survives being put in pure water.
Both kinds of cell have a membrane. The wall is the plant-only one.
Both respire, so both have mitochondria.
Both have a nucleus. Bacteria are the ones without.

options.text: from where there are more of them to where there are fewer
options.feedback: Down the concentration gradient, with no energy needed. Osmosis is a special case of exactly this.

options.text: from where there are fewer of them to where there are more
options.feedback: That direction needs energy, and it is called active transport. Diffusion goes the other way.

options.text: only when the cell uses energy from respiration
options.feedback: Diffusion is free: it is just molecules moving about at random and spreading out.
Diffusion happens anywhere molecules are free to move, including in air and in liquids with no cell in sight.

items.stem: Complete the sentence. Osmosis moves water molecules across a selectively permeable membrane…
items.skill: State the definition the specification gives

options.text: out of the dilute solution and into the more concentrated one
options.feedback: That is the specification's wording. Water goes to where there is less of it.

options.text: out of the more concentrated solution and into the dilute one
options.feedback: That is the direction the sugar would go if it could fit through. Water moves the other way: towards the more concentrated solution.

options.text: out of the dilute solution and into the more concentrated one, using energy from respiration
options.feedback: The direction is right, but osmosis needs no energy — it is a kind of diffusion. Energy from respiration belongs to active transport.

options.text: between two solutions of equal concentration
options.feedback: Between equal concentrations there is no net movement at all, so nothing would change.

items.stem: A carrot cylinder is left in pure water. What happens to its mass, and why?
items.skill: Predict the direction of water movement

options.text: It increases, because water moves into the cells by osmosis
options.feedback: Pure water is the most dilute solution there is, so water moves into the cell sap.

options.text: It decreases, because water moves out of the cells by osmosis
options.feedback: Water moves towards the more concentrated solution, and that is the cell sap inside the carrot, not the pure water outside.

options.text: It increases, because sugar moves into the cells from the water
options.feedback: There is no sugar in pure water, and sugar molecules are too large to cross the membrane anyway. Only the water moves.

options.text: It stays the same, because the cell wall stops water entering
options.feedback: The wall limits how much water can enter, which is why the cell does not burst, but water does get in and the mass does rise.

items.stem: In a plasmolysed plant cell, which structure has moved?

options.text: the cell membrane, which has pulled away from the cell wall
options.feedback: That is the sentence the scheme wants: the membrane pulls away from the wall.

options.text: the cell wall, which has pulled away from the membrane
options.feedback: The wall is rigid and stays where it is. It is the membrane, with the shrinking contents, that comes away from it.

options.text: the nucleus, which has moved into the vacuole
options.feedback: The nucleus is not what the question is about. Look at the outside of the cell contents: the membrane has left the wall.

options.text: nothing has moved; the whole cell has simply shrunk
options.feedback: The contents shrink, but the wall does not, and the gap that opens between them is the point of the word plasmolysed.

items.stem: A cylinder starts at 4.50 g and finishes at 4.86 g. What is the percentage change in mass?
items.skill: Calculate a percentage change in mass

options.feedback: Change ÷ starting mass × 100 = 0.36 ÷ 4.50 × 100.
That is the change divided by the FINAL mass. A percentage change is always measured against the mass you started with.
That is the change in grams, not a percentage. Divide it by the starting mass and multiply by 100.
Starting mass minus final mass gives the change the wrong way round. The cylinder gained mass here, so the answer is positive.

items.stem: Why does a plant cell in pure water become turgid rather than bursting?
items.skill: Give the role of the cell wall

options.text: The strong cell wall limits how much water can enter
options.feedback: Once the wall is pushed out as far as it will go, no more water can get in. That is the wall's job in this topic.

options.text: The cell membrane stops any more water entering
options.feedback: The membrane is selectively permeable and lets water through freely. It is the wall outside it that limits the entry of water.

options.text: The vacuole stores the extra water safely
options.feedback: The vacuole does fill up, but it is the wall that stops the cell expanding any further and bursting.

options.text: Plant cells do not take in water by osmosis
options.feedback: They do, and that is why they become turgid. What the wall changes is the ending, not the process.

items.stem: A red blood cell is placed in pure water. What happens to it?
items.skill: Contrast an animal cell with a plant cell

options.text: Water enters by osmosis and the cell bursts
options.feedback: An animal cell has no cell wall, so nothing limits the water entering and the membrane splits.

options.text: Water enters by osmosis and the cell becomes turgid
options.feedback: Turgid is a plant-cell word: it needs a wall for the contents to press against. An animal cell simply swells until it bursts.

options.text: Water leaves by osmosis and the cell shrinks
options.feedback: Pure water is more dilute than the cytoplasm, so water moves in, not out. It shrinks in a concentrated solution instead.

options.text: Nothing happens, because the membrane is not permeable to water
options.feedback: The membrane is selectively permeable, and water is exactly the molecule it lets through.

items.stem: A cylinder starts at 5.60 g and finishes at 5.18 g. What is the percentage change in mass?
items.skill: Calculate a signed percentage change from the starting mass

options.feedback: −0.42 ÷ 5.60 × 100 = −7.5, signed for a loss.
That divides by the final mass, 5.18; the divisor is the mass at the start.
That is the change in grams; divide it by the starting mass and multiply by 100.
The cylinder lost mass, so the change is negative.

the distilled water is more dilute than the cell sap, so water moves into those cells
that cylinder gains mass, and its cells become turgid as the vacuole pushes the membrane against the wall
the cell wall limits the entry of water, so the plant cells do not burst

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Two cylinders, and for each one: which way the water moves, what happens to the mass, and what happens to the cells.
The two words that separate a Band A answer from a Band B one are turgid and plasmolysed.
parts.workedSolution: Osmosis moves water molecules across a selectively permeable membrane, out of the dilute solution and into the more concentrated one. Distilled water is more dilute than the cell sap of the carrot cells, so water moves into those cells. The cylinder in distilled water therefore gains mass, and its cells become turgid: the vacuole fills and pushes the cytoplasm and membrane against the cell wall. The strong cell wall limits how much water can enter, so the cells do not burst. The 0.8 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution is more concentrated than the cell sap, so water moves out of the cells in the second cylinder. That cylinder loses mass, and its cells become flaccid and then plasmolysed, with the cell membrane pulling away from the cell wall.

commonErrors.feedback: The osmosis is there but the cells are not. Band A needs the state of the cells in both cylinders: turgid in the water, plasmolysed in the sucrose.

parts.workedSolution: Dissolving rock salt makes the soil solution more concentrated than the cell sap inside the root cells. findings.asked: A potato core in a concentrated sugar solution: explain the change in the liquid level and describe the cells.
findings.wentWrong: Many misread the question and wrote about concentration rather than the level; a general definition of osmosis earned nothing - the answer had to say water leaves the potato and where it goes. Some thought 'smaller' could not be used twice (vacuole and cytoplasm both shrink); few could answer about the cell membrane.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Traced the water: from the dilute potato cells, through the partially permeable membranes, into the concentrated solution outside, so the level rises.
findings.rule: Apply osmosis to this situation: which way the water moves and what that does.

findings.asked: Red blood cells in salt solutions of different concentrations; then why potato cells behave differently.
findings.wentWrong: Measuring and picking the matching concentration were fine; the explanation was the most discriminating item on the paper, with many writing the definition or a muddled account, and few linked the potato cell wall to limiting how much water can enter.
findings.rule: Animal cells burst or shrivel; plant cells become turgid or plasmolysed because the wall stops them bursting.

insight.ruleToRemember: Osmosis is the movement of water through a partially permeable membrane from a dilute to a more concentrated solution. In the exam, name the direction for the situation given and its effect (level, mass, length, turgid or plasmolysed); the cell wall is why plant cells do not burst.
insight.aStarSignal: Explaining a novel set-up (Visking tubing, blood cells, potato chips) with the direction of water movement, the reason, and the consequence in one clear chain.
